message.content:
### Your Rights as a Tenant in Texas (as of 2026) | Area | What You’re Entitled To | How to Exercise It | |------|------------------------|--------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • The landlord may hold a maximum of **one month’s rent** (or two if the lease is for a furnished unit).
• The deposit must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | • Keep a copy of the lease and any move‑in inspection report.
• Request a written itemized statement of deductions if the landlord withholds part of the deposit. | | **Habitability** | • The landlord must keep the premises in a safe, sanitary, and livable condition (e.g., functioning plumbing, heating, electrical, pest control). | • Report problems in writing (email or certified mail) and give the landlord a reasonable time to fix them.
• If the issue is serious (e.g., no heat in winter), you may withhold rent or repair and deduct, but only after following the proper notice procedures. | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are limited to **$25** or **5%** of the rent, whichever is greater. | • Pay on time or negotiate a payment plan if you’re experiencing hardship. | | **Entry Rights** | • Landlord must give **at least 24 hours’ written notice** before entering, except in emergencies. | • Keep a log of all entries. If the landlord enters without notice, you can refuse entry and document the incident. | | **Privacy** | • You have the right to quiet enjoyment of the premises. The landlord cannot harass or interfere with your privacy. | • Report any harassment to the landlord in writing; if it continues, consider filing a complaint with the Texas Attorney General’s Office or local housing agency. | | **Discrimination** | • Landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income (e.g., public assistance). | • File a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). | | **Lease Termination** | • Either party may terminate a month‑to‑month lease with **30 days’ written notice**.
• For fixed‑term leases, the landlord must provide a valid reason for early termination (e.g., breach of lease). | • Keep copies of all notices. If the landlord terminates without cause, you may sue for damages. | | **Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major defect after notice, you may repair it yourself and deduct the cost from rent, but only after giving the landlord a **reasonable** notice period. | • Keep receipts and document the defect. | | **Eviction Process** | • The landlord must serve a **3‑day notice** for non‑payment of rent or a **30‑day notice** for lease violations.
• After the notice period, the landlord can file an eviction lawsuit. | • Respond to the lawsuit promptly; you can contest the eviction in court. | | **Fair Housing** | • You’re protected under the Texas Property Code and federal Fair Housing laws. | • If you suspect discrimination, file a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights or HUD. | | **Utilities** | • The lease should specify who pays utilities. If not, the landlord must provide a written statement of who is responsible. | • Keep utility bills as proof of payment. | | **Subletting** | • The lease may prohibit subletting or require landlord approval. | • Obtain written permission before subletting; otherwise, you risk lease violation. | | **Maintenance of Common Areas** | • Landlord must maintain common areas (e.g., hallways, elevators) in a safe condition. | • Report issues in writing; keep a record of your communication. | --- #### Practical Steps to Protect Your Rights 1. **Read Your Lease Carefully** - Look for clauses on security deposits, maintenance responsibilities, entry notice, and termination. 2. **Document Everything** - Keep copies of all communications (emails, texts, letters). - Take photos or videos of any maintenance issues. 3. **Use Written Notices** - Whenever you need to notify the landlord (e.g., repair request, rent payment, notice of termination), send a written notice via certified mail or email with read receipt. 4. **Know the Timeline** - Texas law sets specific time frames for notice and response. Stick to them to avoid losing rights. 5. **Seek Legal Advice if Needed** - If you face eviction, discrimination, or a dispute over the security deposit, consider consulting a tenant‑rights attorney or a local legal aid organization. 6. **File Complaints When Appropriate** - For discrimination: Texas Commission on Human Rights or HUD. - For landlord harassment or unlawful eviction: Texas Attorney General’s Office or local housing authority. --- #### Quick Reference: When to Call a Lawyer | Situation | Why You Might Need a Lawyer | |-----------|-----------------------------| | Landlord refuses to return your security deposit without a valid deduction | To recover the deposit and possibly damages | | Landlord attempts to evict you without following proper notice or court procedure | To contest the eviction and protect your housing | | You suspect discrimination in housing | To file a formal complaint and seek remedies | | You’re unsure whether a lease clause is enforceable | To interpret the lease and advise on your rights | --- **Remember:** These rights are general guidelines. Specific situations can vary, especially if your lease contains unique clauses or if you’re in a city with additional ordinances (e.g., Austin’s rent‑control or eviction protections). Always check the most recent Texas Property Code and local regulations.
